## Package orientation

---
description: 'Ready-made AI tools and MCP client/server support: `mcp`, `serve`, `webSearchTool`, `fetchUrlTool`, `httpRequestTool`, `calculatorTool` and `dateTimeTool`; also mounts `ai.mcp` and `ai.tools`. Use for "connect an MCP server", "serve tools over MCP", "search the web" or "fetch a URL". # @warlock.js/ai-tools

A belt of prebuilt tools for `@warlock.js/ai` agents plus the Model Context Protocol bridge in both directions. Importing the package attaches `ai.tools.*` and `ai.mcp` onto the shared `ai` object; the factories are also exported directly.

## The 80% path

1. Give an agent web or API access with the factories (`use-web-and-http-tools.md`); pass the results in the agent's `tools` array.
2. Consume tools from an external MCP server (`connect-mcp-server.md`); they arrive as normal agent tools.
3. Publish your own tools to MCP clients such as editors or agent CLIs, over stdio or a loopback HTTP endpoint with a bearer token (`expose-as-mcp-server.md`).

## Conventions and pitfalls

- Direction A (`connect-mcp-server.md`) consumes; Direction B (`expose-as-mcp-server.md`) serves. Do not mix them up.
- `fetchUrlTool` and `httpRequestTool` are policy-gated: set host allowlists and byte caps rather than opening them fully.
- `webSearchTool` needs a search provider choice and its API key (tavily, brave, or serpapi).
- Every error class extends the `AIError` of `@warlock.js/ai`; catch by subclass.
- Writing a custom tool with `ai.tool()` is covered by the `define-ai-tool` topic of the `@warlock.js/ai` package.


## connect-mcp-server  `@warlock.js/ai-tools/skills/connect-mcp-server/SKILL.md`

Skip: exposing YOUR agent/tools AS an MCP server (the reverse direction) — the `expose-as-mcp-server` topic; the built-in web/HTTP/calc/date tools — the `use-web-and-http-tools` topic.'

# Connect to an external MCP server (Direction A)

`ai.mcp(server, options?)` opens a connection to any Model Context Protocol server, lists its tools, and adapts each one into a native `ToolContract` — so a remote MCP tool is indistinguishable from a local one and drops straight into `ai.agent({ tools: [...] })`.

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";

const github = ai.mcp(
  { type: "stdio", command: "npx", args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"] },
  { namePrefix: "github." },
);

const dev = ai.agent({
  model,
  systemPrompt: "Use the GitHub tools to triage issues.",
  tools: [...(await github.tools())], // handshake + tools/list, run once and cached
  maxTrips: 20,
});

await dev.execute("Find the oldest open 'bug' issue and propose a fix.");

await github.close(); // on teardown — kills the child / ends the HTTP session
```

## The transport — `stdio` or `http`

The `server` argument is discriminated by `type`:

```ts
// Spawn a child process and speak JSON-RPC over its stdin/stdout.
// Uses node:child_process + node:readline — NO dependency.
{ type: "stdio", command: "npx", args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"], env: { GITHUB_TOKEN: "…" } }

// Streamable HTTP against an endpoint.
{ type: "http", url: "https://mcp.example.com/rpc", headers: { authorization: "Bearer …" } }
```

> **stdio env is not inherited.** When you pass `env`, only those keys reach the child — pass what the server needs (e.g. its API token) explicitly.

## Client options

```ts
ai.mcp(server, {
  namePrefix: "github.", // prepended to every remote tool name
  filter: (name) => name.startsWith("issues_"), // only adapt tools whose name passes
  timeoutMs: 30_000, // per tools/call deadline (default 30s)
  signal: controller.signal, // optional: close the client when this aborts
});
```

- **`signal`** binds the client's lifetime to a run: on abort the client closes its transport (kills the stdio child / ends the HTTP session), in-flight requests reject, and later `tools()` / tool calls fail with `McpTransportError` type `"closed"` without sending anything. Each `tools/call` honors it together with the per-call `ctx.signal` — whichever aborts first. `close()` stays idempotent.

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai, type ModelContract } from "@warlock.js/ai";

export async function triage(model: ModelContract): Promise<void> {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const github = ai.mcp(
    { type: "stdio", command: "npx", args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"] },
    { namePrefix: "github.", signal: controller.signal },
  );

  const agent = ai.agent({ model, tools: [...(await github.tools())] });
  await agent.execute("Triage the open issues", { signal: controller.signal });

  controller.abort(); // ends the run AND shuts the MCP server down
}
```

- **`namePrefix`** is the collision mitigation — there is **no runtime tool-name collision guard** (the agent resolves a tool by first name match), so the author owns uniqueness. Prefix remote tools to keep them distinct from local ones.
- **`filter`** receives each tool's _unprefixed_ name; return `false` to drop it.

## What `tools()` does

`client.tools()` is lazy and cached: the **first** call runs the `initialize` handshake, sends `notifications/initialized`, then `tools/list`, and maps each descriptor into a `ToolContract`. Repeat calls return the cached array without re-handshaking.

For each remote tool:

1. its JSON-Schema `inputSchema` is wrapped as a Standard Schema via `jsonSchemaToStandard` (Ajv-backed — `ajv` is an optional peer needed only for the client), which also exposes that schema (`~standard.jsonSchema`) so the model sees the server's real argument names;
2. `execute` issues `tools/call` honoring `ctx.signal` (cooperative abort) and the configured `timeoutMs`, then unwraps the result content (a single JSON text block is parsed back into an object);
3. an MCP `isError` result is thrown so the surrounding `tool()` wraps it as a `ToolExecutionError` — the agent reads it as `{ error }` data and self-corrects.

### Selecting one discovered tool

When selecting one discovered tool, guard the array result before invoking it.
A server may advertise no tools, and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` reflects that:

```ts
import type { McpClient } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";

export async function invokeFirst(client: McpClient, input: unknown) {
  const [contract] = await client.tools();
  if (!contract) throw new Error("The MCP server advertised no tools");
  return contract.invoke(input);
}
```

## `type`, never `kind`

MCP's wire vocabulary uses `kind` in some content/capability descriptors. The client translates any inbound `kind` to `type` when normalizing content blocks, so a value a tool returns never carries MCP's `kind` — every discriminator the agent sees is `type`.

## Errors

Connection / handshake failures surface **at agent-construction time** because the example `await`s `github.tools()` — you see them then, not mid-run. A `tools/call` failure raised mid-run is wrapped by `tool()` and reaches the model as data. Branch on `McpTransportError.type`:

```ts
import { McpTransportError } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";

try {
  await github.tools();
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof McpTransportError && error.type === "connect") {
    // the child failed to spawn, the endpoint was unreachable, or the handshake failed
  }
}
```

`McpTransportError.type`: `"connect"` | `"protocol"` | `"timeout"` | `"closed"` (plus an optional `.method` naming the in-flight JSON-RPC method).

## Optional peers

The MCP client does not use `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`: it speaks MCP's JSON-RPC itself, over a spawned child process (`node:child_process`) for `{ type: "stdio" }` and the global `fetch` for `{ type: "http" }`, so neither transport needs a dependency. Its only optional peer is `ajv`, which validates tool-call input against each MCP tool's `inputSchema`. It is imported lazily the first time a schema is checked; when it is missing, the call fails validation with a curated `npm install ajv` message instead of crashing at import time. A tool with no `inputSchema` needs no validator.

## See also

- The `expose-as-mcp-server` topic — the reverse direction: publish a local primitive AS an MCP server.
- The `use-web-and-http-tools` topic — the built-in web / HTTP / calculator / date-time belt.
- The `run-ai-agent` topic of the `warlock-js-ai` skill — running the agent that consumes the adapted tools.

Triggers: `ai.mcp.serve(`, `serve(`, `createServeHandler`, `McpServer`, `McpServeOptions`, `McpServeSource`, `McpServeTransport`, `McpHttpServeTransport`, `McpHttpAuth`, `onAuthRefusal`, `McpHttpAuthRefusal`, `McpServeError`, `server.start()`, `server.stop()`, `{ url, close }`, `{ type: "http", host, port, path, auth }`, `bearer`, `authorize`, `authenticate`, `beforeCall`, `listFilter`, `validateCallParams`, `McpError`, `routes`, `McpHttpRouteContext`, `requestId`, `principal`, `notifications/cancelled`, `allowedOrigins`, `maxBodyBytes`, `prefixToolNames`, `groups`, `resources`, `prompts`, `ctx.request.headers`, `schemaTarget`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `{ type: "stdio" }`; ''expose my agent as an MCP server'', ''serve my tools over HTTP'', ''give each agent session its own MCP endpoint'', ''protect my MCP server with a token'', ''publish my tools to Cursor/Claude Desktop'', ''serve MCP resources or prompts'', ''tool name collision''; typical import `import "@warlock.js/ai-tools"; import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai"`. # Expose tools AS an MCP server (Direction B)

`ai.mcp.serve(source, options)` turns a local set of `ToolContract`s into a Model Context Protocol server — so Cursor, Claude Desktop, a coding CLI, or any MCP client can call your warlock tools / agent. Transports: **stdio** (default) and MCP **Streamable HTTP**.

## Serve over HTTP with a per-session token

```ts
import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";

const token = randomBytes(32).toString("hex");

const server = ai.mcp.serve([ai.tools.calculator(), ai.tools.dateTime()], {
  name: "session-tools",
  transport: { type: "http", auth: { bearer: token } },
});

const { url, close } = await server.start();
// url → "http://127.0.0.1:<free port>/mcp" — hand url + token to the MCP client

await close(); // drains in-flight calls, then frees the port
```

Defaults: `host: "127.0.0.1"`, `port: 0` (free ephemeral port), `path: "/mcp"`. `start()` resolves `{ url, close }` once bound.

## Serve over stdio

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";

const server = ai.mcp.serve([ai.tools.calculator()], {
  name: "warlock-utils",
  transport: { type: "stdio" },
});

await server.start(); // reads JSON-RPC lines from stdin, answers on stdout
// on teardown:
await server.stop();
```

## HTTP options and security rules

```ts
transport: {
  type: "http",
  host: "127.0.0.1",           // non-loopback (e.g. "0.0.0.0") REQUIRES auth — start() throws otherwise
  port: 0,
  path: "/mcp",
  auth: {
    bearer: ["current-token", "previous-token"], // constant-time compare; several = rotation
    authorize: async (request) => sessions.has(request.headers["x-session-id"] ?? ""), // optional hook
  },
  allowedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"], // besides loopback origins
  allowedHosts: ["mcp.internal"],              // extra Host names while on loopback
  maxBodyBytes: 1_048_576,                     // larger → 413
  drainTimeoutMs: 5_000,                       // close() then aborts ctx.signal
}
```

- Checks run in order: `bearer`, `authorize`, `authenticate`; every configured check must pass. A failed check skips later hooks. `authenticate` alone satisfies the non-loopback auth requirement. Host/Origin checks run first. A throwing authentication hook denies. By default, failures → `401`; bearer or authenticate failures include a Bearer `WWW-Authenticate` challenge.
- A foreign or `null` `Origin` → `403` (DNS-rebinding guard from the MCP spec). Requests without `Origin` pass.
- On loopback, a `Host` other than `localhost` / `127.0.0.1` / `[::1]` (or `allowedHosts`) → `403`.
- Stateless: no session id; `GET` / `DELETE` → `405`; batches → `400`; unsupported `MCP-Protocol-Version` → `400`.
- Plain HTTP: put TLS in front before exposing beyond the machine.

## Customize HTTP authentication refusals

Use `transport.onAuthRefusal` for a JSON error contract shared by the MCP endpoint
and `transport.routes`. It runs only after a failed bearer/authorize/authenticate
check. Host/Origin refusals always take precedence and never call it.

```ts
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";
import type { McpHttpAuthRefusal } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";

const onAuthRefusal: McpHttpAuthRefusal = async ({ check, target }) => ({
  status: 401,
  headers: { "cache-control": "no-store" },
  body: { error: "MEMBER_UNAUTHORIZED", check, target },
});

const server = ai.mcp.serve([], {
  name: "member-tools",
  transport: {
    type: "http",
    auth: { authorize: () => false },
    onAuthRefusal,
    routes: [{ method: "GET", path: "/policy", handler: () => ({ body: {} }) }],
  },
});
const { url, close } = await server.start();
// url and `${url}/policy` share the custom refusal; no handler runs.
await close();
```

- Context has only `check: "bearer" | "authorize" | "authenticate"`, uppercase
  `method`, query-free `path`, and `target: "mcp" | "route"`. No error, credentials,
  headers, principal or request body is passed. Thrown auth details stay private.
- Return `{ status?, headers?, body }` or a promise. Status defaults to 401 and
  must be an integer 400–599. Required body is plain JSON, including primitives,
  arrays and null; no cycles, class instances, non-finite numbers or undefined entries.
- Header allowlist: `www-authenticate`, `cache-control`, `retry-after`,
  `content-language`, `x-request-id`. Public types use lowercase keys; runtime
  matches names case-insensitively and validates HTTP string values. Headers merge
  over the default challenge. Framing, cookies, CORS and redirects cannot be set.
- Void, throws/rejections and any invalid result fall back to the original 401
  JSON-RPC `Unauthorized.` response and default headers. A custom denial cannot
  grant authority: it ends the request without later auth, route, policy or tool
  handlers. Successful auth skips the refusal hook.
- Exported types: `McpHttpAuthRefusal`, `McpHttpAuthRefusalContext`,
  `McpHttpAuthRefusalResponse`, `McpHttpAuthRefusalBody`, `McpHttpAuthRefusalHeader`.

## Tools read request headers from `ctx.request`

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai, type ToolContract } from "@warlock.js/ai";

const whoami: ToolContract = ai.tool({
  name: "whoami",
  description: "Report the calling tenant",
  execute: async (_input: unknown, ctx) => ({
    tenant: ctx?.request?.headers["x-tenant-id"] ?? "unknown",
  }),
});

const { url, close } = await ai.mcp
  .serve([whoami], { name: "tenant-tools", transport: { type: "http" } })
  .start();
```

Header names are lower-cased; every client header is present (including `authorization`). Over stdio `ctx.request` is absent. Nothing on `ctx.request` reaches the model.

## Authenticated context, policy and cancellation

```ts
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import type { McpHttpRequestInfo, McpCallRefusal } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";

declare function findMember(
  request: McpHttpRequestInfo,
): Promise<{ id: string; canCall: boolean } | undefined>;
const denied: McpCallRefusal = {
  isError: true,
  content: [{ type: "text", text: "Member cannot call tools" }],
  _meta: { policy: "membership" },
};
const identity = ai.tool({
  name: "identity",
  description: "Report the authenticated caller and request id",
  execute: async (_input: unknown, ctx) => {
    ctx?.signal?.throwIfAborted();
    return { requestId: ctx?.requestId, principal: ctx?.principal };
  },
});

const server = ai.mcp.serve([identity], {
  name: "member-tools",
  transport: { type: "http", auth: { authenticate: findMember } },
  beforeCall: async (context, tool, input) => {
    const member = context.principal; // unknown — narrow before use
    if (
      typeof member !== "object" ||
      member === null ||
      !("canCall" in member) ||
      member.canCall !== true
    ) {
      return denied;
    }
    // context.requestId: JSON-RPC id; tool: original ToolContract;
    // input: validated data, treated as read-only.
  },
});
```

- `authenticate(request)` may be synchronous or async. `undefined` or a thrown error → `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="mcp"`; every other value becomes `context.principal` and `ctx.principal`. Secrets in thrown auth errors are not exposed.
- `beforeCall(context, tool, input)` runs after schema validation. Return nothing to allow; return `McpCallRefusal` (`isError: true`) to send native content/metadata unchanged, independent of result mode. Throw `McpError` → its own code/message/data; other throws → JSON-RPC `-32602`. Invalid refusals → `-32603`. Invalid input skips policy. The boundary validates before policy and `invoke` keeps its own validation, so schemas must be deterministic and policy input read-only.
- Stdio identity: `transport: { type: "stdio", principal: { id: "local" } }` or `transport: { type: "stdio", principalProvider: async (context) => ({ id: "local", requestId: context.requestId }) }`. The provider runs per request, takes precedence over static principal, and receives the request id and abort signal. A provider throw → JSON-RPC internal error. No HTTP request metadata exists over stdio.
- Public types: `McpBeforeCall`, `McpCallRefusal`, `McpServeToolContext`, `McpStdioServeTransport`; `ToolContext` in `@warlock.js/ai` adds optional `requestId` and `principal`.

[Cancellation (MCP 2025-11-25)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/utilities/cancellation): send `{ jsonrpc: "2.0", method: "notifications/cancelled", params: { requestId: 42, reason: "Caller cancelled" } }`. The matching signal aborts; no JSON-RPC response is sent even if the tool later returns or throws. Unknown/completed/malformed ids are ignored; `initialize` cannot be cancelled. String and numeric ids are distinct; calls sharing an in-flight id still execute, but ambiguous cancellation in one scope is ignored.

HTTP cancellation POSTs must repeat caller credentials and application headers (`Authorization`, `Cookie`, tenant/custom auth headers), from the same remote address. Transport headers such as content length, accept, protocol version and connection may differ. Different credentials can reuse ids safely. Clients sharing credential/application headers must use unique in-flight ids for cancellation to identify a call. Notifications get `202`; a cancelled HTTP call ends with `202`, no JSON-RPC body, when its handler settles. Stdio scopes cancellation to the connection. HTTP disconnect, stdio EOF/close/stop, or HTTP shutdown after the drain timeout also abort tools. Pass `ctx.signal` into cancellable work.

## Control discovery, call envelopes and HTTP side routes

Use this complete example for hidden-but-callable tools, custom protocol errors,
unknown envelope policy, and side routes under the same authentication:

```ts
import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";
import { McpError } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";

const tools = [ai.tools.calculator(), ai.tools.dateTime()];
const token = randomBytes(32).toString("hex");
const canCall = (principal: unknown, name: string) =>
  principal === "member" && tools.some((tool) => tool.name === name);

const server = ai.mcp.serve(tools, {
  name: "member-tools",
  listFilter: async (context, descriptors) =>
    context.principal === "member"
      ? descriptors.filter((entry) => entry.name === "calculator")
      : [],
  validateCallParams: (_context, params) => {
    const unsupported = Object.keys(params).filter(
      (key) => !["name", "arguments", "_meta"].includes(key),
    );
    if (unsupported.length > 0) {
      throw new McpError(-32600, "Unsupported call envelope", { fields: unsupported });
    }
  },
  beforeCall: (context, tool) => {
    if (!canCall(context.principal, tool.name)) {
      throw new McpError(-32600, "Denied");
    }
  },
  transport: {
    type: "http",
    path: "/mcp",
    auth: { bearer: token, authenticate: () => "member" },
    routes: [
      {
        method: "GET",
        path: "/tool-policy",
        handler: (context) => ({
          body: { allowed: canCall(context.principal, context.url.searchParams.get("name") ?? "") },
        }),
      },
    ],
  },
});
const { url, close } = await server.start();
// `${url}/tool-policy?name=date_time` requires the same bearer token.
// date_time stays callable via tools/call, under beforeCall, despite being hidden.
await close();
```

- `listFilter(context, tools)` runs per `tools/list`, on fresh wire descriptors
  with schemas and exposed (possibly prefixed) names. Return a descriptor array,
  possibly empty or reordered. It only affects discovery; call lookup and policy
  are independent. A throwing filter fails that list request, leaving tools callable.
- `validateCallParams(context, params)` runs after the basic object/name check,
  before lookup/schema validation/`beforeCall`/invoke. It sees the full read-only
  params including unknown fields, `_meta` and `task`. Return nothing or throw.
  Both hooks support promises and the same request id/principal/request/signal
  as `beforeCall`, on HTTP and stdio. For stdio, use
  `transport: { type: "stdio", principal: "member" }` with these same hooks.
- `McpError(code, message, data?)` extends `Error`. `beforeCall` and
  `validateCallParams` preserve its integer code, message and optional data in
  JSON-RPC errors. SDK `McpError` is recognized by Error/name/integer code without
  a runtime SDK dependency; its `.message` is preserved including the SDK prefix.
  Other thrown values stay `-32602`; tool execution errors stay `isError: true`.
- Defaults continue ignoring extra envelope fields. The server speaks
  `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and advertises no task capability.
  [MCP 2025-11-25 task handling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/utilities/tasks#task-support-and-handling)
  requires ignoring task metadata without that capability. The example's
  rejection of `task` is an explicit app policy; omit it to retain default behavior.
  Allow `_meta`, which is protocol metadata.
- `transport.routes` is HTTP-only. Host/Origin and all configured bearer,
  authorize and authenticate checks run before body reads/handlers. Auth is
  optional on loopback and required elsewhere, just as for MCP. `context` has
  `request`, `principal`, parsed `url`, raw UTF-8 `body`, `signal`; no request id.
  Route bodies share `maxBodyBytes`. MCP-only JSON/header checks do not apply.
  A handler returns `{ status?: number, headers?: Record<string, string>, body?: unknown }`;
  status defaults to 200, body is JSON, omitted body is empty, HEAD suppresses it.
  Exceptions return a generic 500. Disconnect and shutdown abort the signal;
  routes share `close()` draining. Reuse your policy function explicitly;
  route requests do not invoke `beforeCall`.
- Route suffix `/tool-policy` appends to MCP path `/mcp` or `/mcp/` as
  `/mcp/tool-policy` (root MCP path `/` gives `/tool-policy`). Exact methods:
  GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/HEAD/OPTIONS. No wildcard, automatic HEAD or CORS.
  Query strings do not affect matching; read them with `url.searchParams`.
  Known path + wrong method → 405 with Allow; unknown path → 404.
- Route suffixes require nonempty segments containing letters/digits/`_-.~`.
  Empty suffix, `/`, dot segments, percent escapes, repeated or trailing slashes,
  queries, fragments and wildcards fail start with `McpServeError.type: "config"`.
  With routes, the MCP base must be a canonical pathname. All methods on the
  MCP endpoint are reserved, so routes cannot override it. Duplicate method/path
  pairs fail start with `"collision"`; different methods on a suffix are allowed.
- Public types: `McpListFilter`, `McpValidateCallParams`, `McpHttpRoute`,
  `McpHttpRouteContext`, `McpHttpRouteResponse`.

## Return native MCP results

Default results become one text block, even when an object resembles an MCP result. Return the exported `mcpResult(...)` helper to preserve native content blocks, `isError`, `structuredContent` and `_meta` over stdio or HTTP:

```ts
import { mcpResult } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";

const count = ai.tool({
  name: "count",
  description: "Return a structured count",
  meta: {
    outputSchema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: { count: { type: "number" } },
      required: ["count"],
    },
  },
  execute: async (_input: unknown, ctx) =>
    mcpResult({
      content: [{ type: "text", text: '{"count":2}' }],
      structuredContent: { count: 2 },
      _meta: { tenant: ctx?.request?.headers["x-tenant-id"] ?? "unknown" },
    }),
});

ai.mcp.serve([count], { name: "counts" });
```

The helper returns a branded `McpNativeResult` wrapper. The serving boundary validates and unwraps it without altering its payload. `isError: true` is sent as-is; thrown tool errors retain the existing mapping.

For tools that already return native objects, opt in at the server or tool level:

```ts
const nativeTool = ai.tool({
  name: "native-result",
  description: "Return a native result",
  meta: { mcpResults: "native" }, // this tool opts in even on a default server
  execute: async () => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: "fixture" }], isError: true }),
});

ai.mcp.serve([nativeTool], { name: "native-tools", results: "native" });
// On a native-mode server, meta: { mcpResults: "text" } disables detection for a tool.
// Explicit mcpResult(...) returns always opt in, regardless of the detection setting.
```

Native mode detects objects containing any of `content`, `isError`, `structuredContent` or `_meta`; other values keep text serialization. `content` must be an array of valid MCP text/image/audio/resource-link/embedded-resource blocks. Optional `isError` must be boolean; `structuredContent` and `_meta` must be JSON objects. Invalid or non-JSON native payloads answer a JSON-RPC internal error (`-32603`), including malformed helper payloads.

`meta.outputSchema` is emitted as `outputSchema` in `tools/list`; `structuredContent` passes through unchanged. Tool authors own schema conformity. Follow the [MCP 2025-11-25 tools specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools#structured-content): also include serialized structured output in a text block for compatibility.

Request identity is unchanged: native tools receive each HTTP call's headers and remote address on `ctx.request`, plus `ctx.signal`. Over stdio, `ctx.request` is absent. Returning a native result does not automatically expose request metadata; the tool controls its response.

## Sources and tool-name collisions

```ts
ai.mcp.serve([calc, dt], { name: "utils" }); // literal array
ai.mcp.serve({ tools: () => ws.tools.all() }, { name: "workspace" }); // anything with tools()
ai.mcp.serve(
  { groups: { prod: [search], staging: [search] } },
  {
    name: "search",
    prefixToolNames: true, // → prod_search, staging_search; or (group, name) => `${group}.${name}`
  },
);
```

Duplicate exposed names throw `McpServeError` (`type: "collision"`) **when `serve()` is called**. `prefixToolNames` on an ungrouped source throws `type: "config"`.

## Resources and prompts (optional)

```ts
ai.mcp.serve(tools, {
  name: "handbook",
  resources: [
    {
      uri: "docs://handbook",
      name: "handbook",
      mimeType: "text/markdown",
      read: () => "# Handbook",
    },
  ],
  prompts: [
    {
      name: "review",
      arguments: [{ name: "diff", required: true }],
      get: (args) => `Review this diff:\n${args.diff ?? ""}`, // string → one user message
    },
  ],
});
```

`read()` returns a string (text) or `Uint8Array` (base64 blob). `get()` returns a string or `McpPromptMessage[]`. Unknown resource → `-32002`; unknown prompt / missing required argument → `-32602`.

## How the protocol maps

- **`initialize`** → `{ name, version }`, capabilities `tools` (+ `resources` / `prompts` when configured); protocol version negotiated from `SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS` (`2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`).
- **`tools/list`** → `inputSchema` via `extractJsonSchema(contract.input, { target: schemaTarget })` (default `"draft-2020-12"`).
- **`tools/call`** → `invoke()`; default `data` → text block (JSON-stringified unless a string), opted-in native results → validated passthrough, `error` → `isError: true`. Unknown tool → JSON-RPC error.
- **`ping`** → `{}`.

## Drive the protocol yourself (tests, custom servers)

```ts
import { createServeHandler } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";

const handler = createServeHandler([ai.tools.calculator()], { name: "utils" });

const response = await handler.handle(
  { jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 1, method: "tools/list" },
  { request: { method: "POST", path: "/mcp", headers: { "x-tenant-id": "acme" } } },
);
```

Mounting it in your own server means you own Origin validation, auth and body limits.

## Errors

`McpServeError.type`: `"collision"` (from `serve()`), `"config"` (unsafe/invalid options, from `start()`), `"listen"` (bind failed). Bad requests never throw — they get an HTTP status or JSON-RPC error; failing tools return `isError: true`.

## use-web-and-http-tools  `@warlock.js/ai-tools/skills/use-web-and-http-tools/SKILL.md`

name: use-web-and-http-tools
description: 'Wire the @warlock.js/ai-tools belt — web search, fetch/scrape, HTTP/REST, calculator, date-time — into an agent under their guardrails. Triggers: `ai.tools.measure`, `measureTools`, `ai.tools.webSearch`, `ai.tools.fetchUrl`, `ai.tools.http`, `ai.tools.calculator`, `ai.tools.dateTime`, `webSearchTool`, `fetchUrlTool`, `httpRequestTool`, `calculatorTool`, `dateTimeTool`, `web_search`, `fetch_url`, `http_request`, `calculator`, `date_time`, `WebToolError`, `HttpPolicyError`, `CalculatorError`, `DateTimeError`, `allowHosts`, `allowMethods`, `allowPrivateNetwork`, `baseUrl`, `maxBytes`, `guardedFetch`, `SearchProvider`, `TAVILY_API_KEY`; ''give an agent web search'', ''let an agent fetch/scrape a page'', ''let an agent call a REST API'', ''restrict which hosts/methods an agent can hit'', ''add a calculator/date tool to an agent'', ''SSRF guardrail for an agent tool'', ''let a tool reach an internal/dev service''; typical import `import "@warlock.js/ai-tools"; import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai"`. # Use the web + HTTP tool belt

`@warlock.js/ai-tools` ships five ready-made tools. Import the package once for its side effect and they register on the shared `ai` object under `ai.tools.*` — each is a factory returning a `ToolContract` you spread into `ai.agent({ tools: [...] })`.

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai } from "@warlock.js/ai";
import { OpenAISDK } from "@warlock.js/ai-openai";

const openai = new OpenAISDK({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY! });

const agent = ai.agent({
  model: openai.model({ name: "gpt-4o" }),
  systemPrompt: "Research, then call the API. Read tool errors and adjust.",
  tools: [
    ai.tools.webSearch({ provider: "tavily" }),
    ai.tools.fetchUrl({ extract: "text", allowHosts: ["docs.stripe.com"] }),
    ai.tools.http({ baseUrl: "https://api.stripe.com", allowHosts: ["api.stripe.com"] }),
    ai.tools.calculator(),
    ai.tools.dateTime({ defaultTimeZone: "UTC" }),
  ],
  maxTrips: 15,
});
```

The construction `options` are the **rails** — they bound what the model may do; the model supplies the per-call inputs _within_ those rails. Least-privilege is just array composition: hand an agent only the tools (and only the methods/hosts) it needs.

## The five tools

| Factory                         | Name           | Model input                                                    | Returns                                          |
| ------------------------------- | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `ai.tools.webSearch(options)`   | `web_search`   | `{ query, maxResults? }`                                       | `{ results: { title, url, snippet, score? }[] }` |
| `ai.tools.fetchUrl(options?)`   | `fetch_url`    | `{ url }`                                                      | `{ url, status, content, truncated }`            |
| `ai.tools.http(options?)`       | `http_request` | `{ method?, url, headers?, body? }`                            | `{ status, headers, body, truncated }`           |
| `ai.tools.calculator(options?)` | `calculator`   | `{ expression }`                                               | `{ result }`                                     |
| `ai.tools.dateTime(options?)`   | `date_time`    | `{ op, iso?, from?, to?, amount?, unit?, timeZone?, format? }` | `{ value }`                                      |

## `web_search` — pick a provider, supply a key

```ts
ai.tools.webSearch({ provider: "tavily", apiKey: process.env.TAVILY_API_KEY, maxResults: 8 });
```

- `provider`: `"tavily"` (LLM-ready snippets + a relevance `score`), `"brave"`, or `"serpapi"`. Each is called over the global `fetch` — **no provider SDK is required**.
- `apiKey` falls back to a per-provider env var: `TAVILY_API_KEY` / `BRAVE_API_KEY` / `SERPAPI_API_KEY`. A missing key is a `WebToolError` of type `"missing-key"`.
- The model's `maxResults` is clamped into `[1, options.maxResults]` (default `5`).

## `fetch_url` — read a page you have the URL for

```ts
ai.tools.fetchUrl({
  extract: "text",
  allowHosts: ["docs.stripe.com"],
  maxBytes: 500_000,
  timeoutMs: 10_000,
});
```

- `extract`: `"text"` (default — readability-extracted main text), `"html"` (raw body), or `"markdown"`. **`"text"`/`"markdown"` lazily import the `@mozilla/readability` + `jsdom` optional peers** — a missing peer is a `WebToolError` of type `"missing-peer"` carrying the `npm install @mozilla/readability jsdom` string. `"html"` needs nothing.
- `allowHosts` (when set) rejects any other host **before the fetch** (an SSRF guardrail) → `"denied-host"`, and redirect targets are held to the same allowlist.
- **Private-network deny by default.** Every request — and every redirect hop — now routes through `@warlock.js/ai`'s hardened `guardedFetch` outbound policy instead of a local host check. It refuses private / loopback / link-local / CGNAT / cloud-metadata addresses (`169.254.169.254`, RFC1918, `localhost`, …) by resolving the hostname via DNS and checking every returned address, failing closed on resolution failure — and re-validates every redirect `Location` (scheme, allowlist, private-IP deny) before following it. This applies even with no `allowHosts` set, so a bare `ai.tools.fetchUrl()` is no longer an SSRF primitive; blocks surface as `WebToolError` `type: "denied-host"`.
- `allowPrivateNetwork` (default `false`) — set `true` to deliberately permit a private/internal target, e.g. a tool that must call a local dev server. Pair with `allowHosts` to scope it rather than opening the whole private range.
- `maxBytes` caps the body and flags `truncated`; `timeoutMs` aborts via `AbortSignal.timeout`.

## `http_request` — a guarded REST client

```ts
ai.tools.http({
  baseUrl: "https://api.stripe.com",
  allowHosts: ["api.stripe.com"],
  allowMethods: ["GET", "POST"], // default ["GET"] — mutating methods are opt-in
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.STRIPE_KEY}` },
  timeoutMs: 15_000,
  maxBytes: 1_000_000,
  // allowPrivateNetwork: true,             // only for a deliberate internal/dev target
});
```

All guardrails are enforced **before the network call** and surface as a typed `HttpPolicyError`:

- a method outside `allowMethods` → `"method-not-allowed"`;
- a host outside `allowHosts` → `"host-not-allowed"` (SSRF guardrail);
- an unresolvable URL → `"invalid-url"`.
- **Private-network deny by default** — like `fetch_url`, every request and redirect hop routes through `guardedFetch`, refusing private/loopback/link-local/CGNAT/cloud-metadata addresses (DNS-resolved and re-checked per redirect hop) even when `allowHosts` isn't set → `"host-not-allowed"`. Set `allowPrivateNetwork: true` (default `false`) to permit a deliberate internal target.

When `baseUrl` is set the model passes a **path** joined against it; otherwise it must pass an absolute `http(s)` URL. Static `headers` merge **under** the per-call headers (per-call wins). An object `body` is JSON-serialized (with a default `content-type: application/json`); a string `body` is sent verbatim; `body` is dropped for `GET`. The response body is JSON-parsed when the `content-type` is JSON, else returned as text.

## `calculator` — SAFE arithmetic (never `eval`)

```ts
const { data } = await ai.tools.calculator().invoke({ expression: "(3 + 4) * 2 ^ 3" });
data?.result; // 56
```

Supports `+ - * / % ^`, unary signs, parentheses, and decimal/scientific literals, with the usual precedence (`^` highest and right-associative). The expression is tokenized and evaluated with a shunting-yard pass — there is no path to an identifier, function call, or property access, so nothing code-like can be smuggled in. Failures are a `CalculatorError`: `"syntax"`, `"divide-by-zero"`, or `"overflow"`.

## `date_time` — clock + calendar

```ts
await ai.tools.dateTime().invoke({ op: "now", format: "iso" });
await ai.tools
  .dateTime()
  .invoke({ op: "add", iso: "2026-06-22T00:00:00Z", amount: 3, unit: "days" });
await ai.tools
  .dateTime()
  .invoke({ op: "diff", iso: "2026-06-22T00:00:00Z", to: "2026-06-25T00:00:00Z", unit: "days" }); // "3"
await ai.tools
  .dateTime({ defaultTimeZone: "Africa/Cairo" })
  .invoke({ op: "format", iso: "2026-06-22T12:00:00Z", format: "datetime" });
```

- `op`: `"now"` / `"add"` / `"diff"` / `"format"`. `format`: `"iso"` (default), `"date"`, `"time"`, `"datetime"`.
- For `diff`, pass the start instant as `iso` **or** `from` (an alias models reach for naturally with `from`/`to`); `iso` wins when both are set. The end instant is always `to`.
- Units are millisecond-based: `milliseconds`, `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks` (plus singular/short aliases like `day`/`d`). Calendar-relative `month`/`year` are intentionally **unsupported** — they have no fixed length. An unknown unit → `DateTimeError` `"invalid-unit"`; an unknown IANA zone → `"invalid-time-zone"`.
- For deterministic tests, inject a clock by calling the factory directly: `import { dateTimeTool } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools"; dateTimeTool({}, { clock: () => Date.parse("2026-06-22T00:00:00Z") })`.

## `ai.tools.measure` — what the belt costs per model call

`ai.tools.measure(tools, options?)` is `measureTools` from `@warlock.js/ai`: the input tokens a tool list adds to every call, per tool and in total. Native and exact when the model has `countTokens` (`source: "native"`, `tools.length + 2` count calls, `overhead` = the provider's once-per-request tool preamble); estimated from the schema JSON otherwise (`source: "estimate"`).

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai, type ModelContract } from "@warlock.js/ai";

export async function reportBeltCost(model: ModelContract): Promise<void> {
  const belt = [ai.tools.calculator(), ai.tools.dateTime()];

  const full = await ai.tools.measure(belt, { model });
  const compact = await ai.tools.measure(belt, { model, mode: "compact" });

  console.log(full.source, full.tokens, "→", compact.tokens, full.perTool);
}
```

If compact saves enough, run the agent with `toolSchemas: "compact"` (the `define-ai-tool` topic of the `warlock-js-ai` skill).

## Errors flow as data, not throws

Every failure above is thrown inside the tool handler, caught by the framework's `tool()` wrapper, and surfaced in the returned `{ error }` field — `invoke()` never throws, so the agent reads the failure as a `role: "tool"` message and self-corrects on the next trip. Each error class extends the `@warlock.js/ai` `AIError` base; branch on `.type`:

```ts
import { WebToolError } from "@warlock.js/ai-tools";

const { error } = await ai.tools
  .fetchUrl({ allowHosts: ["docs.stripe.com"] })
  .invoke({ url: "http://evil.test" });
if (error instanceof WebToolError && error.type === "denied-host") {
  // rejected before any network call
}
```

## Add the belt to a discovery catalogue

Registration extends the core namespace, preserving `ai.tools.catalogue` and `ai.tools.measure`:

```ts
import "@warlock.js/ai-tools";
import { ai, type ModelContract } from "@warlock.js/ai";

declare const model: ModelContract;
const surface = ai.tools.catalogue({
  core: [ai.tools.calculator()],
  searchable: [ai.tools.dateTime()],
  limit: 8,
});
const assistant = ai.agent({ model, tools: surface.tools });
const measured = await ai.measure({ model, tools: surface.tools });
console.log(measured.parts.tools.tokens);
```

The core plus `tool_search` / `tool_call` stays advertised. Hidden calls still traverse target policy, approval, validation, accounting and tracing. The `define-ai-tool` topic covers lazy descriptors, ranking and measurement comparisons. Native provider tools stay alongside the catalogue; eager ones included in its lists pass through unchanged and are excluded from discovery.
